name: United States
tagline: Four years, no major on day one, and no such thing as the American deadline
summary: An American bachelor's degree takes four years and starts broad: you take courses across several fields and usually declare a major at the end of year two. Almost everything else about applying is set by the institution rather than by the country. There is no ministry of education that decides who qualifies, no national recognition body that converts an IB Diploma into anything, no minimum points, and no single deadline — the University of California closes on 30 November 2026 for a degree starting in autumn 2027, Harvard's regular round closes on 1 January 2027, Yale's on 2 January and MIT's on 4 January, and MIT is not on the same application form as any of them. What decides how you apply here is which application system your institution uses and what kind of institution it is. It is not which state it is in.
whyConsider: You do not have to choose your subject before you arrive — you can start in autumn 2027 and declare a major in 2029.

A small group of very wealthy private universities and liberal arts colleges meet 100% of assessed financial need for international students. Harvard states plainly that international students are eligible for exactly the same aid as Americans and that families earning under 100,000 USD pay nothing.

Higher Level results can convert into real course credit. The University of California publishes a rate card — 8 quarter units per HL exam at 5, 6 or 7, plus 6 for the diploma itself at 30 points or more — which is worth about a term of a four-year degree.

Liberal arts colleges are small, taught by professors rather than teaching assistants, and are often more generous to international students than the famous research universities. Several charge no application fee at all.

The community-college transfer route — two years at an Associate degree, then two years at a university — is the cheapest way into an American bachelor's degree and almost no IB student is told it exists.
watchOuts: There is no American deadline. Among the fourteen institutions in this profile the regular round closes on 30 November, 1 January, 2 January, 4 January, 5 January and 15 January, and the early round runs from 1 to 15 November. Carrying one institution's date to another is the single most expensive mistake available here, because nothing reopens afterwards — there is no Clearing, no late round and no second intake.

An IB Diploma removes nothing by itself. Yale requires the SAT or ACT from every applicant and states that IB results may accompany the score but not replace it; MIT requires it too. Harvard accepts IB actual or predicted scores only where testing is genuinely inaccessible, which Copenhagen is not. If a selective university is on your list, book a test date in 2026.

Early Decision is a contract, not a preference. Amherst's wording is that you agree not to be an Early Decision candidate anywhere else and, if admitted, to withdraw your applications from other colleges and enrol. It raises your odds and it ends your ability to compare financial aid offers, which for a family paying from Denmark is usually the more expensive loss.

Financial aid is applied for with the application, not after it. Grinnell requires every aid form by the application deadline; Macalester states that aid cannot be awarded after an offer of admission has been made, and not at any later point in the degree either.

What an IB Diploma is worth in credit varies from a full term to nothing, at institutions that are equally official about it. An HL Physics 6 is 8 quarter units at Berkeley and zero at MIT, which gives credit only at grade 7 and none at all for IB Biology or Chemistry. Read the credit page of every institution on your list before you apply.

Health insurance is compulsory, expensive and charged automatically. Every registered Berkeley student including international students is enrolled in the campus plan unless they waive it; in Massachusetts it is state law. A Danish policy may be comprehensive and still fail the waiver because it is not accessible where you are living.

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: There is no national minimum, because there is no national rule and no body empowered to make one. The United States has no federal ministry of education with authority over admission and no recognition body of the kind the European destinations in this dataset have — each institution decides for itself what an IB Diploma is worth, both for entry and for credit. The nearest thing to a published threshold found here is the University of California's credit rule, which awards diploma credit at 30 points or above; that is a credit floor at one system, not an entry requirement anywhere.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: Higher Level is what counts. Every credit rule found here is written about Higher Level exams and Standard Level earns nothing: the University of California awards 8 quarter units per HL exam graded 5, 6 or 7, and MIT restricts credit to Higher Level at grade 7 only. For entry rather than credit, admissions committees read the rigour of the subject choice as part of a holistic file rather than checking it against a list, so there is no equivalent of a subject requirement to satisfy.
ibRecognition.gradeConversion: There is no national IB-to-GPA conversion and no body that could publish one. Institutions read the IB transcript directly — predicted grades at the application stage, actual results afterwards. Where a conversion of any kind exists it is a credit conversion at one institution: the University of California awards 6 quarter units (4 semester units) for a full IB Diploma scored 30 or above, plus 8 quarter units (5.3 semester) for each Higher Level exam graded 5, 6 or 7, usually 24 quarter units in total.
notes: MIT is the other pole and is equally official: Higher Level only, grade 7 only, no credit at all for IB Biology, Chemistry or Information Technology in a Global Society, 18.01 for HL Mathematics at 7 and 8.01 for HL Physics at 7. Two official American pages, the same diploma, and outcomes that differ by a term of study.
Yale requires the ACT or SAT from all first-year applicants and says IB scores may be included "along with" that score. Along with, not instead of.

Harvard requires the SAT or ACT and names IB Actual or Predicted Scores as an alternative only "in exceptional cases when those tests are not accessible". This is a hardship provision, not an IB exemption.

Your school sends predicted grades; final results arrive on 6 July 2027, after every American decision in the cycle. Offers are made on predictions plus everything else in the file. The University of California is unusually explicit about the other end of it and wants official IB results by 15 July 2027.
What an institution does if the final results fall below the predictions is set by that institution and is not established here. Ask before you accept a place.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: Everything. The question is not whether the degree is in English but whether you must prove your English.
language.englishProof: Set per institution and not by any national rule. Many waive a TOEFL or IELTS for an applicant taught in English, which an IB Diploma normally demonstrates, but the waiver is not automatic — Arizona State publishes an English-proficiency requirement for international applicants with no IB exemption named. Ask each institution in writing whether your IB English result satisfies it.
notes: Your IB English A result is the strongest evidence you can offer, and it is evidence rather than an entitlement.

feeContext.summary: At a public university a Danish student pays the non-resident rate for all four years, because residency for tuition is not something an F-1 student acquires by living in the state. The University of California publishes both figures for 2027–28: UC Tuition of 16,278 USD for a California resident and 57,300 USD for a nonresident, with a total on-campus cost of attendance of 49,078 and 90,100 USD. UC also holds its tuition line flat for up to six years under a Tuition Stability Plan. The non-resident figures for Michigan, Illinois and Arizona State are not established here.

At a private university or liberal arts college there is one published price for everyone and the real question is how much of it is discounted. Harvard's 2025–26 billed cost was 86,926 USD, with health insurance a further 4,308 USD — and Harvard also states that international students are eligible for exactly the same aid as Americans, that it meets 100% of demonstrated need and that families earning under 100,000 USD contribute nothing. Between those two extremes sit institutions like Grinnell, which considers your need when deciding whom to admit and then meets 100% of it for those it takes. The aid application is due with the admission application, and Macalester states that aid cannot be awarded after an offer has been made.

livingContext.healthcare: Compulsory, expensive, and charged to the bill automatically rather than offered. Every registered UC Berkeley student, international students included, is enrolled in the campus plan at 2,533 USD per semester for undergraduates in 2026–27 unless they waive it with proof of comparable cover. In Massachusetts it is state law: Harvard states that Massachusetts law requires any full-time or part-time student at an institution of higher learning in the state to hold qualifying student health insurance or comparable cover, and its waiver closes on 31 July. A Danish travel or study policy may be comprehensive and still fail, because a waiver also requires the cover to be reasonably accessible where you are living.
livingContext.residency: There is no free movement of any kind. After you accept an offer the institution issues Form I-20, you pay the 350 USD I-901 SEVIS fee, complete the DS-160 and attend an F-1 visa interview at the US Embassy in Copenhagen, bringing the SEVIS receipt with you.

sectorLandscape.summary: American higher education has no ministry and no national structure, so the sectors are not legal categories — they are recognisable kinds of institution with different sizes, prices, admission behaviour and purposes, and the names below are the ones Americans actually use. A full IB Diploma opens all of them. The two that most IB students are never told about are at opposite ends: the liberal arts college, which is small, teaching-led and often the most generous to international students, and the community college, which is the cheapest way into an American bachelor's degree and is almost invisible in the English-language advice a Danish student will read.

routes.what: Endowed, independent of any state government, and running graduate schools alongside the undergraduate college — Harvard, Yale, Stanford, NYU. One published price for everyone, which is very high, discounted by need-based aid that at a handful of them is extraordinarily generous to international applicants and at most of them is not offered to them at all. Admission is holistic, opaque and at the famous names in the low single digits for international applicants.
routes.note: The sector English-language advice is almost always describing when it says "applying to America", and the sector a realistic list cannot be built entirely out of.

routes.what: Small — often 1,500 to 2,500 students — almost always residential, undergraduate only, with no graduate students competing for a professor's attention and classes taught by professors rather than teaching assistants. Amherst runs an open curriculum with no distribution requirements at all. The breadth-then-depth shape is closer to the IB Diploma than anything else in the United States, and several of these colleges are more generous to international students, and cheaper to apply to, than the research universities: Colby charges no application fee.
routes.note: Habitually mistaken for a lesser option by students who have never heard of the names. They are as selective as the Ivies and they are where a student who wants to be taught rather than lectured should be looking.

routes.what: Owned by a state and built to educate its residents — Michigan, Illinois, Berkeley, Arizona State. Large, strong in engineering and the sciences, and priced in two tiers: a resident rate and a non-resident rate that a Danish student pays for all four years. Institutional aid for international students is limited or absent; Michigan states that international students on temporary visas should expect to pay the full cost of attendance. These are also the institutions where the application route is least predictable, because some are on the Common App and some are on their own state system.
routes.note: The sector where the difference between 16,278 and 57,300 USD a year is decided by something a foreign student cannot acquire.

routes.what: Two-year institutions awarding an Associate of Arts or Associate of Science, with open or flexible admission, small classes and fees a fraction of a university's. The point for a foreign student is the "2+2": two years at a community college followed by two years at a university, leaving with the university's bachelor's degree. Six University of California campuses — Davis, Irvine, Merced, Riverside, Santa Barbara and Santa Cruz — operate a Transfer Admission Guarantee that turns the second half into a published promise rather than a hope.
routes.note: The cheapest route into an American degree and the one nobody mentions. Recorded with an explicit gap: whether an F-1 student from Denmark can hold a Transfer Admission Guarantee on the same terms as a Californian resident is not established here, and nobody should plan around it until it is.

routes.what: Science and engineering institutions with a common technical core — MIT is the archetype. Everyone takes the same mathematics and physics in the first year, the pace assumes strong Higher Level mathematics, and the admission process is often run outside the shared application systems entirely.
routes.note: Also the sector most likely to give an IB student nothing for their Higher Level results. MIT grants credit only at grade 7 and none at all in Biology or Chemistry.

routes.what: Independent schools of art, design, music, dance and theatre, admitting on portfolio or audition. Grades matter less, the portfolio matters more than anything else, and the calendar and the supplementary steps are different from everything else in this Destination — Stanford's arts-supplement deadline, for example, falls two to four weeks ahead of the ordinary one.
routes.note: Not researched in detail here. Recorded because it exists and because a student who needs it will not find it in the ordinary listings.

routes.what: Degree-granting institutions run as businesses, marketed heavily to international students and to adult learners, with admission requirements that are often nominal.
routes.note: Recorded because it exists and because it is the part of the sector a student searching online will meet first. Nothing about its accreditation, its transferability, its visa status or its value has been researched here, and it should not be treated as advised for or against until it has been.

jurisdictions.name: The Common App colleges
jurisdictions.summary: Twelve of the fourteen institutions here, spread across all ten states in this profile, on one form. A private research university in Massachusetts and a public flagship in Illinois are on exactly the same application with exactly the same submission items; what differs between them is the round they offer, the date they close and whether they require a test. This is the group that shows why grouping the United States by state would have told a student nothing.

variations.label: There is no shared date inside this group
variations.summary: Early Decision closes between 1 and 15 November 2026 (Macalester 1st, Amherst 9th, Bowdoin and Grinnell 15th). Early Action closes on 1 November 2026 everywhere that runs one. Regular Decision closes on 1 January (Harvard), 2 January (Yale), 5 January (Stanford, Amherst, Illinois) and 15 January (Grinnell) — and Illinois wants the school's documents a further week later. Everyone replies on 1 May 2027.

variations.label: One price, or two
variations.summary: This group mixes private colleges, where there is a single published price for everyone and the question is how much aid discounts it — Harvard's 2025–26 billed cost was 86,926 USD — with three public universities, Michigan, Illinois and Arizona State, where a Danish student pays a non-resident rate for all four years. The non-resident figures for those three are not established here, because all three refused automated retrieval or do not publish them on the pages we could read. Application fees also vary inside the group from nothing at Colby to 100 USD at Stanford.

variations.label: Massachusetts makes it law
variations.summary: Health insurance is compulsory at every institution in this group, but in Massachusetts — Harvard and Amherst here — it is a state requirement rather than an institutional one: Harvard states that Massachusetts law requires any full-time or part-time student at an institution of higher learning in the state to participate in a qualifying student health insurance programme or a plan of comparable coverage. The waiver window closes on 31 July, before a student has arrived, and comparable cover must be reasonably accessible where you are living.

variations.label: Tests are required at some and optional at others
variations.summary: Yale requires the ACT or SAT from every applicant and will not take IB results instead; Harvard requires it with a narrow hardship exception. New York University, Michigan and Amherst are test-optional, and Michigan and NYU ask for one teacher reference or none where others ask for two. One application form, four different sets of requirements behind it.

jurisdictions.name: The University of California
jurisdictions.summary: A genuine sub-national admissions authority, and the clearest case in this Destination of a boundary that is not a state line: nine campuses, one application, one filing window, one set of rules set by the Regents rather than by the campus. Berkeley is the campus in this profile and adding the other eight costs only the fee. Everything a student learns about applying to the Common App colleges has to be unlearned here.

variations.label: One window, five weeks before everyone else
variations.summary: The fall 2027 application opens on 1 August 2026, is filed between 1 and 30 November 2026, and is not accepted a day either side. There is no Early Decision, no Early Action, no rolling consideration and no late round. Decisions arrive across March 2027, the Statement of Intent to Register is due on 1 May 2027, and official IB results must reach the campus by 15 July 2027 — nine days after the IB publishes them.

variations.label: Resident and non-resident tuition, and which one you pay
variations.summary: For 2027–28 UC publishes UC Tuition of 16,278 USD for a California resident and 57,300 USD for a nonresident, a gap of a little over 41,000 USD a year, with total on-campus costs of 49,078 and 90,100 USD. A Danish student is a nonresident and stays one — residency for tuition is not something an F-1 student acquires by living in California. The one piece of good news is the Tuition Stability Plan, which holds the tuition line flat for up to six years.

variations.label: Enrolled in the campus plan automatically
variations.summary: Every registered UC Berkeley student, international students included, is automatically enrolled in the Berkeley Student Health Insurance Plan, which cost undergraduates 2,533 USD per semester in 2026–27 and can only be left by proving comparable insurance during an annual waiver window. Two semesters at that rate is more than a year's total living costs in several European destinations. The 2027–28 rate is not published yet.

variations.label: No references, four short essays, and a published credit rate
variations.summary: UC does not require or read letters of recommendation at the time of application; a campus may ask later in a supplemental review. Instead of one long personal essay there are four personal insight questions of 350 words. And UC publishes what the IB is worth in credit, which almost nothing else in this Destination does: 6 quarter units for a diploma at 30 points or above and 8 quarter units per Higher Level exam graded 5, 6 or 7.

jurisdictions.name: Institutions that take only their own application
jurisdictions.summary: Applying directly is a route, not the absence of one, and MIT is its best-known practitioner: it has never joined the Common App and does not intend to. A student who builds the whole autumn around one portal will discover in October that MIT is not in it. Only one of the fourteen institutions here sits in this group; the wider American population of direct-only institutions has not been surveyed.

variations.label: Its own calendar, and it is not the common one
variations.summary: Early Action closes 1 November with decisions in mid-December; Regular Action closes 4 January, not the 1 January most American guidance quotes. The financial aid application is separate from the admissions application and falls after it — 30 November for Early Action and 15 February for Regular Action. MIT also dates its testing requirement to the sitting rather than the score report: before 30 November for Early Action, before 31 December for Regular Action.

variations.label: The SAT or ACT is required, and the IB is worth very little in credit
variations.summary: MIT requires the SAT or ACT with no IB alternative. Its credit rule is the narrowest found anywhere in this Destination: Higher Level exams only, grade 7 only, no credit at all for IB Biology, Chemistry or Information Technology in a Global Society, 18.01 for HL Mathematics at 7, 8.01 for HL Physics at 7 and nine units of unrestricted elective credit per applicable humanities, arts or social science exam.

variations.label: Massachusetts again
variations.summary: MIT is in Massachusetts, where state law requires students at institutions of higher learning to hold qualifying student health insurance or comparable cover. MIT's own plan cost, waiver terms and waiver deadline are not established here; the Massachusetts requirement is recorded only as Harvard states it, because the state regulation itself refused automated retrieval.

notes: Grouped by application environment rather than by state, and the argument is worth keeping: fourteen institutions across ten states would have produced ten groups, seven of them holding a single institution, and the state would have predicted nothing. Harvard and MIT are both in Cambridge, Massachusetts and are on different application systems with different deadlines; Michigan and Berkeley are both public flagships and are on different systems too. What actually decides how a student applies here is the shared application system, which cuts across states, so that is the boundary the record declares. Declaring "none" would have been false — the University of California closes five weeks before everyone else and runs no early round at all.

The Coalition Application on Scoir and the QuestBridge Application are named by Yale, Amherst and Bowdoin as equal alternatives to the Common App. Neither has a record of its own yet. Neither is anybody's only route among these fourteen, which is why they are not separate jurisdictions.
ApplyTexas, Cal State Apply and the SUNY application are further shared applications in this Destination and are unresearched, because none of the fourteen institutions in this profile uses one.

Deadlines for New York University, the University of Michigan and Colby College are not recorded. All three sites refuse automated retrieval — HTTP 405, 403 and 403 respectively, from both the fetch tool and a browser user agent — so all three are placed on a route from the Common App's own member directory and nothing further is claimed about them. This is a gap to close by hand, not an absence of requirements.
Bowdoin's own pages disagree about its Regular Decision date. Recorded as a conflict on ev-bowdoin-dates and deliberately not resolved.

Arizona State's priority date for fall 2027 was not published when this was checked on 23 September 2026, so the profile carries it as not-yet-announced rather than inferring one. Recheck from about December 2026.

Not established: whether an F-1 student from Denmark can hold a University of California Transfer Admission Guarantee on the same terms as a California resident. This is the question the community-college route turns on and the per-campus TAG matrix was not opened.

Not established: the non-resident tuition figures for Michigan, Illinois and Arizona State; MIT's health-plan cost and waiver terms; and what any institution does when final IB results fall below the predicted grades an offer was made on.
Programme-level records not yet created. Stages 1–5 of the research brief are done for this Destination; stage 6 is not.
